title: Theory, Limits and Practice
intro: What a quantum reservoir can and cannot compute, what it costs as it grows, where a quantum advantage could come from, and a complete reservoir you can run in numpy.

blocks.text: The earlier chapters of this shelf describe how a quantum reservoir is built and how to use one. This chapter asks what such a machine can and cannot do. Four questions organise it. Which input-output maps can the output approximate at all (expressivity)? How much of the exponentially large state space survives measurement with a finite number of shots (concentration and scalability)? When, if ever, does any of it beat a classical model of the same cost (advantage)? And how does one build and test one in a few dozen lines of code (practice)? The fifth page lists what is still unknown.

The chapter is the most mathematical on the shelf, but it is written for the same reader as the rest: you need high-school algebra, the idea of a derivative, and the earlier pages. Every result is derived step by step with numbers, and every claim about a simulated reservoir comes from a script you can run.

Read Getting Started (#/qrc/start) first, in particular A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand) (a complete reservoir worked by hand) and Training, Testing and Measuring Error (#/qrc/start/training-and-testing) (how readouts are trained and scored). You will also want the reservoir model of The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir) (the reset encoding that this chapter analyses), the echo state property (The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property)) and memory capacity (Memory and Processing Capacity (#/qrc/foundations/memory-and-capacity)). From the Quantum Mechanics shelf (Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum)) the pages on mixed states, tensor products and the partial trace are used throughout.

Every quantum reservoir on this shelf, whatever its hardware, is the same mathematical object: an input-driven quantum channel followed by a linear readout. The state is updated once per input, the features are expectation values, and only the readout weights are trained:

blocks.caption: The input-driven channel $\mathcal{T}_s$ (completely positive and trace preserving for each input $s$), the measured observables $O_i$, and the trained readout $(w, b)$.

blocks.text: The order to read it in

items: Expressivity and Universality (#/qrc/theory/expressivity-and-universality) (about two hours). Fading-memory filters and Volterra series; why the reset encoding gives features built from $1$, $s$ and $\sqrt{s(1-s)}$; how extra uploads enlarge that family; the Stone–Weierstrass route to universality; and the counting bounds on features and capacity. Start here.

Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability) (about an hour and a half). The variance $1/(2^n+1)$ of a Pauli expectation under scrambling, derived; the shots needed to read a feature; noise as a second source of concentration; the effective number of features; restart costs; what classical simulation costs.

Quantum Advantage (#/qrc/theory/quantum-advantage) (about two hours). Three meanings of advantage, the arguments for and against, a free-fermion reservoir simulated for 200 qubits in well under a second, a NARMA2 case study against polynomial baselines, and a checklist for fair comparison.

Hands-on Implementation (#/qrc/theory/hands-on-implementation) (about two hours, mostly running code). A complete numpy simulator, piece by piece, with tests, memory capacity, shot noise, NARMA2, the expressivity check, damping and trajectories. You can read it first if you prefer to learn from code, and return to the other pages for the reasons.

Open Problems (#/qrc/theory/open-problems) (about an hour). The unanswered questions, each with what is known, a small calculation that shows why it is hard, and a research plan a laptop can start on; plus a self-test across the shelf.

blocks.text: Allow about eight to ten hours in total, spread over several sittings. The first three pages depend on each other in the order shown; the hands-on page can be done at any point after the first.

items: Fading memory plus a point-separating family closed under products gives universality. With the echo state property and product reservoirs (tensor products, whose expectation values multiply), the outputs are dense in the fading-memory filters, by the Stone–Weierstrass argument Boyd and Chua used for Volterra series. This is existence, not efficiency.

Features are linear in $\rho_k$, so the readout can never use more than $4^n - 1$ independent directions per time step, and the total information-processing capacity is bounded by the number of linearly independent features.

The input enters only through how $\mathcal{T}_s$ depends on $s$. With reset encoding, $\mathcal{T}_s = \mathcal{T}_0 + s\,\mathcal{T}_1 + \sqrt{s(1-s)}\,\mathcal{T}_2$, so every output is a sum of products over past steps of functions in $\mathrm{span}\{1, s, \sqrt{s(1-s)}\}$: rich in cross-time products, poor in single-input nonlinearity.

If the dynamics scramble like a random unitary, a Pauli expectation's spread over inputs falls as $1/\sqrt{2^n+1}$, so the shots needed to read it grow as $2^n$. A large Hilbert space is not a large usable feature space.

blocks.text: How to work through the chapter

Each page ends with problems whose solutions are written out step by step. Do the check-yourself questions as you go; they are short. Run each script: the outputs quoted on the pages are from actual runs, and changing a parameter is the quickest way to find out whether you understand a result. If a page seems to rely on something you do not remember, the prerequisite line at its start names where to look.

When you finish, you should be able to read a paper claiming a quantum reservoir result and ask the right questions: what function class does its encoding reach, how many independent features are read and at what shot count, what is the strongest classical baseline of the same size, and how many random draws were averaged?
